records.bodyText:
Ministers have cited independent scientists to justify new rules governing Scotland’s booming data centre industry while refusing to reveal what those experts actually told them, campaigners have revealed.
The Scottish Government has redacted in full the substantive advice it received from the Scottish Science Advisory Council (SSAC) before introducing a new 50MW threshold at which proposed data centres require an Environmental Impact Assessment.
The documents, obtained through freedom of information request by Stop Climate Chaos Scotland (SCCS), confirm that officials consulted the independent scientific body over the threshold shortly before the new rule was introduced.
But the Government has withheld the scientists’ recommendations, meaning the public cannot establish whether they supported the eventual 50MW figure.
Public Finance Minister Hannah Mary Goodlad previously said the rule had been developed “with input from the Scottish Science Advisory Council”.
Fraser Sutherland, coalition manager at SCCS, said: “Ministers told communities that independent scientists shaped the new data centre rules. They now refuse to show the public a single line of what those scientists said.
(Image: Apatura)
“People facing hyperscale data centres on their doorsteps deserve to know whether the 50MW threshold has scientific backing. If the advice supports the government's approach, there is no reason to hide it.”
The released correspondence shows officials sent SSAC a paper marked “Official-sensitive” and asked the body to treat it in confidence.
.On September 9, SSAC provided advice produced by a short-life working group, described by its chair as “high level outputs, provided at pace”.
An “Immediate” briefing on the scientific advice was sent to the minister the following day, and the new 50MW direction was issued on September 16.
But the Government has redacted the advice, the questions posed to SSAC and the briefing subsequently given to the minister.
READ MORE:
7 reveals from Government AI data centre information request
The Future of AI and Data Centres: a deep dive series
Can communities benefit from hyperscale data centre boom?
It has relied on exemptions covering internal communications and personal data and said disclosure could “undermine or constrain” its consideration of policy which remained “under discussion and development”.
SCCS contests that argument, pointing out that the 50MW EIA rule is already in force.
Kat Jones, director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, a rural charity that has campaigned against hyperscale data centres, said: "There is absolutely no reason at all that scientific advice received by Ministers on hyperscale AI data centres should not be in the public domain.
"The secrecy surrounding this information makes it look like the government has something to hide. They should immediately release this advice and any other advice and reports they have received so their decision making can be properly scrutinised.
"Taken together with other information know by government that has come to light in the past couple of weeks, it shows how important it is for them to halt the plans to rush out guidance by Christmas. The Scottish Government must set up an independent and transparent process for researching what impacts hyperscale AI data centres will have on Scotland, the grid, climate targets, land and local communities. And all this information should be published before any guidance or strategic approach is produced."
(Image: PA)
The row comes as Scotland faces a surge of proposed data centre developments, accompanied by concerns over their electricity consumption, impact on the power network and implications for communities and the environment.
It also comes weeks after First Minister John Swinney restated the importance of transparency in government.
Writing in the foreword to the Scottish Ministerial Code published on October 2, Swinney said “citizens rightly expect transparency in decision-making”. The code states that information should not be withheld from the public “unless there are clear and lawful reasons”.
Sutherland said: “The EIA rules are already in force, so there is no live policy debate left to protect.
“Six weeks ago the First Minister told the public they rightly expect transparency in decision-making. His government has now hidden the science behind a new national planning rule.”
SCCS has called for the SSAC recommendations to be published in full.
Its environmental information request was submitted on October 9. The statutory deadline for a response was November 6, but the Government replied on November 12 and apologised for the delay.
The Scottish Government said it held no correspondence between SSAC and ministers or special advisers over data centres. It also said the scientific council did not contribute to the separate notification direction for data centre applications or the Programme for Government's strategic approach to green data centres.
A Scottish Government spokesperson said: “Scotland’s freedom of information laws are the strongest in the UK and the Scottish Government has responded to more than 3,800 FoI and EIR requests since the start of this year, with more than 96% on time.
“Exemptions do apply to Freedom of Information and environmental information, including where disclosure would make available internal communications and where the public interest is served by protecting uninhibited discussion of policy development within government.
”The Scottish Government will be publishing new planning guidance on data centres before the end of the year and, in parallel, is developing a strategic approach to maximise the economic and public benefit from data centre investment in Scotland.”

records.bodyText:
Thirty hyperscale AI data centres planned for Scotland could raise [household energy bills](https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/all-about/fuel-bills) by over £300 a year it has been warned.
Researchers from the [Scottish Greens](https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/all-about/scottish-green-party) calculate the controversial schemes will require so much power they would raise wholesale electricity prices across the UK due to increased demand on the grid.
A Sunday Mail investigation has also uncovered a briefing from the Scottish Parliament’s own research centre which reveals just one of the proposed developments - the 600MW monster site in Auchtertool, Fife - would consume the same [energy](https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/all-about/energy) as 1.6million households.  https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/.../controversial-ai-data...

An animal rescue charity were called to Turriff after six swans died after flying into overhead power lines.
New Arc Wildlife Rescue posted to social media confirming that a flock of Whooper swans had been killed near the River Deveron north of Turriff on Sunday morning.
The discovery was made by the land owner, who lost power to his property.
Animal rescue officers attended the scene, but five of the birds were already dead, and the sixth was severely injured that the officers decided euthanasia was the only humane option. https://news.stv.tv/north/six-swans-die-after-being-electrocuted-by-overhead-power-lines-in-aberdeenshire

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
The Hidden Waste Challenge of Wind Energy 
Wind turbines are often presented as a symbol of a cleaner energy future, but there is another side to the story: what happens when they reach the end of their working lives?
Many turbine blades have an expected lifespan of around 20–30 years. As installations from the 2000s and 2010s approach retirement, recycling and disposal of these large composite structures will become an increasingly important challenge.
A greener future must consider not only how energy is produced, but also what happens to the materials when the technology reaches the end of its life.
The scale of the problem is not merely hypothetical. A UK government review cites global projections ranging from over 2 million to 30–44 million tonnes of blade waste by 2050, depending on the study and assumptions. assets.publishing.service.gov.uk +1
The question is simple: if we're building a greener future today, are we planning responsibly for the waste it could leave behind tomorrow?
#WindEnergy #RenewableEnergy #Environment

The Auchtertool Action Group recently wrote to all the elected MSP for the area asking them to seek answers from ministers to the following questions:
1. When did the Scottish Government first become aware of the findings contained within the May 2026 Scottish Enterprise Report?
2. What action, if any, has been taken in response to each of the seven key points identified?
3. Why have these concerns not been given greater public attention?
4. Has the potential economic and social damage to Scotland been properly assessed?
5. What discussions have taken place within Government regarding the recommendations and warnings contained in the report?
6. What assurances can you give that these issues will not simply be ignored or allowed to worsen?
7. Will you raise these concerns directly with the relevant Cabinet Secretary and seek a formal response from the Scottish Government?
It is encouraging to see Murdo Fraser MSP has lodged the following question. 
“To ask the Scottish Government what elements of the Frazer-Nash report on hyperscale data centres ministers have considered in developing Scotland’s approach to such developments.”
PARLIAMENT.SCOT The Scottish Parliament
